“Let us have faith that right makes might.” — Abraham Lincoln

We often think of strength as something that comes first: authority, money, numbers, influence, or the ability to impose a decision. Lincoln reverses that order. What is right can itself become a source of strength.

But conviction matters only when it shapes conduct. Tell the truth when silence would be easier. Admit a mistake. Refuse to support an unfair decision. In moments like these, principle stops being an opinion and starts becoming character.

Lincoln spoke these words at Cooper Union on February 27, 1860.

“Let us have faith that right makes might.” — Abraham Lincoln

Being right is not yet the same as being strong. Strength appears when a principle actually shapes what we do — especially when silence, compromise, or retreat would be easier.

Lincoln’s words point to a demanding kind of integrity: alignment between what we believe is right and the decisions we are willing to make.
